+---
+type: Specification
+title: Publishing
+description: What a publish writes, the deploy-hook contract an author sees, the retry policy, and why there's no in-app undo.
+---
+
+# Publishing
+
+Publishing a post is three steps, in order:
+
+1. Write a `revisions` row — a snapshot of the post's title and body at the
+   moment of publish.
+2. Flip the post's `status` to `published`.
+3. Call the site's `deployHookUrl`.
+
+The first two are one transaction: either both happen or neither does. The
+third is best-effort. A site's deploy hook is usually a webhook on someone
+else's static host (Vercel, Netlify and similar all expose one), and those
+are occasionally slow or briefly unavailable — worth a retry, not worth
+losing the author's published content over.
+
+## What a failed hook does and doesn't do
+
+By the time the hook call runs, the post and its revision are already
+committed. A failed hook never undoes either: the post stays `published` and
+its revision stays recorded even when every retry fails. See
+[what the Revisions screen shows for a publish like this](./revisions.md#publishing-and-a-failed-hook).
+
+The publish response carries `deployTriggered: boolean`, and the editor
+shows the author which case they're in rather than pretending publish either
+fully succeeded or fully failed.
+
+## Retry policy
+
+The hook gets three attempts, with a linear backoff between them (250ms,
+then 500ms). That's tuned for a cold serverless function taking a moment to
+wake up, not for a target that's genuinely down — three attempts a few
+hundred milliseconds apart won't save a publish from a deploy hook that's
+been deleted or misconfigured. When every attempt fails, the API logs the
+exhaustion at `error` and returns `deployTriggered: false` rather than
+throwing, so the route above always gets a definite answer either way.
+
+This app makes no promise about how long after a successful hook call the
+site itself goes live — that's the host's own build pipeline, which this app
+has no visibility into and no control over.
+
+## There is no unpublish
+
+There's no unpublish action in this cut of the product. The revision a
+publish writes is a record of what went out, not an undo mechanism:
+reverting live content means editing the post back to the previous
+revision's text and publishing again, which writes a new revision rather
+than erasing the old one.

+type: Specification

+---
+
+# Revisions
+
+The Revisions screen lists every revision for a site, grouped by the post
+each one belongs to. Each group's heading uses the post's current title;
+each row uses the title that was saved at the moment of that publish, so
+renaming a post afterward doesn't rewrite what an older row says it
+published.
+
+A draft save updates the post without writing a revision. Only a publish
+adds one.
+
+## Ordering
+
+Revisions are listed newest first within a post. Two publishes in the same
+second are ordinary — the API breaks the tie by revision id, descending, so
+the more recently written revision still sorts first even when its
+timestamp exactly matches an earlier one.
+
+## Publishing and a failed hook
+
+A post becomes `published` together with the revision that snapshots it, in
+one transaction. A failed deploy hook doesn't touch either: the post stays
+published and its revision stays in place even when the site itself didn't
+rebuild. See [the publish contract and what a failed hook means](./publishing.md#what-a-failed-hook-does-and-doesnt-do)

+---
+type: Specification
+title: Publishing
+description: What a publish writes, the deploy-hook contract an author sees, the retry policy, and why there's no in-app undo.
+---
+
+# Publishing
+
+Publishing a post is three steps, in order:
+
+1. Write a `revisions` row — a snapshot of the post's title and body at the
+   moment of publish.
+2. Flip the post's `status` to `published`.
+3. Call the site's `deployHookUrl`.
+
+The first two are one transaction: either both happen or neither does. The
+third is best-effort. A site's deploy hook is usually a webhook on someone
+else's static host (Vercel, Netlify and similar all expose one), and those
+are occasionally slow or briefly unavailable — worth a retry, not worth
+losing the author's published content over.
+
+## What a failed hook does and doesn't do
+
+By the time the hook call runs, the post and its revision are already
+committed. A failed hook never undoes either: the post stays `published` and
+its revision stays recorded even when every retry fails. See
+[what the Revisions screen shows for a publish like this](./revisions.md#publishing-and-a-failed-hook).
+
+The publish response carries `deployTriggered: boolean`, and the editor
+shows the author which case they're in rather than pretending publish either
+fully succeeded or fully failed.
+
+## Retry policy
+
+The hook gets three attempts, with a linear backoff between them (250ms,
+then 500ms). That's tuned for a cold serverless function taking a moment to
+wake up, not for a target that's genuinely down — three attempts a few
+hundred milliseconds apart won't save a publish from a deploy hook that's
+been deleted or misconfigured. When every attempt fails, the API logs the
+exhaustion at `error` and returns `deployTriggered: false` rather than
+throwing, so the route above always gets a definite answer either way.
+
+This app makes no promise about how long after a successful hook call the
+site itself goes live — that's the host's own build pipeline, which this app
+has no visibility into and no control over.
+
+## There is no unpublish
+
+There's no unpublish action in this cut of the product. The revision a
+publish writes is a record of what went out, not an undo mechanism:
+reverting live content means editing the post back to the previous
+revision's text and publishing again, which writes a new revision rather
+than erasing the old one.

+# Revisions
+
+The Revisions screen lists every revision for a site, grouped by the post
+each one belongs to. Each group's heading uses the post's current title;
+each row uses the title that was saved at the moment of that publish, so
+renaming a post afterward doesn't rewrite what an older row says it
+published.

+A draft save updates the post without writing a revision. Only a publish
+adds one.

+
+Revisions are listed newest first within a post. Two publishes in the same
+second are ordinary — the API breaks the tie by revision id, descending, so
+the more recently written revision still sorts first even when its
+timestamp exactly matches an earlier one.
+
+## Publishing and a failed hook
+
+A post becomes `published` together with the revision that snapshots it, in
+one transaction. A failed deploy hook doesn't touch either: the post stays
+published and its revision stays in place even when the site itself didn't
+rebuild. See [the publish contract and what a failed hook means](./publishing.md#what-a-failed-hook-does-and-doesnt-do)

+# Publishing

+   moment of publish.
+2. Flip the post's `status` to `published`.

+third is best-effort. A site's deploy hook is usually a webhook on someone

+losing the author's published content over.

+fully succeeded or fully failed.

+   moment of publish.
+2. Flip the post's `status` to `published`.
+3. Call the site's `deployHookUrl`.

+third is best-effort. A site's deploy hook is usually a webhook on someone
+else's static host (Vercel, Netlify and similar all expose one), and those
+are occasionally slow or briefly unavailable — worth a retry, not worth
+losing the author's published content over.

+

+committed. A failed hook never undoes either: the post stays `published` and
+its revision stays recorded even when every retry fails. See

+shows the author which case they're in rather than pretending publish either
+fully succeeded or fully failed.

+then 500ms). That's tuned for a cold serverless function taking a moment to
+wake up, not for a target that's genuinely down — three attempts a few
+hundred milliseconds apart won't save a publish from a deploy hook that's

+exhaustion at `error` and returns `deployTriggered: false` rather than
+throwing, so the route above always gets a definite answer either way.

+---
+type: Specification
+title: Publishing
+description: What a publish writes, the deploy-hook contract an author sees, the retry policy, and why there's no in-app undo.
+---
+
+# Publishing
+
+Publishing a post is three steps, in order:
+
+1. Write a `revisions` row — a snapshot of the post's title and body at the
+   moment of publish.
+2. Flip the post's `status` to `published`.
+3. Call the site's `deployHookUrl`.
+
+The first two are one transaction: either both happen or neither does. The
+third is best-effort. A site's deploy hook is usually a webhook on someone
+else's static host (Vercel, Netlify and similar all expose one), and those
+are occasionally slow or briefly unavailable — worth a retry, not worth
+losing the author's published content over.
+
+## What a failed hook does and doesn't do
+
+By the time the hook call runs, the post and its revision are already
+committed. A failed hook never undoes either: the post stays `published` and
+its revision stays recorded even when every retry fails. See
+[what the Revisions screen shows for a publish like this](./revisions.md#publishing-and-a-failed-hook).
+
+The publish response carries `deployTriggered: boolean`, and the editor
+shows the author which case they're in rather than pretending publish either
+fully succeeded or fully failed.
+
+## Retry policy
+
+The hook gets three attempts, with a linear backoff between them (250ms,
+then 500ms). That's tuned for a cold serverless function taking a moment to
+wake up, not for a target that's genuinely down — three attempts a few
+hundred milliseconds apart won't save a publish from a deploy hook that's
+been deleted or misconfigured. When every attempt fails, the API logs the
+exhaustion at `error` and returns `deployTriggered: false` rather than
+throwing, so the route above always gets a definite answer either way.
+
+This app makes no promise about how long after a successful hook call the
+site itself goes live — that's the host's own build pipeline, which this app
+has no visibility into and no control over.
+
+## There is no unpublish
+
+There's no unpublish action in this cut of the product. The revision a
+publish writes is a record of what went out, not an undo mechanism:
+reverting live content means editing the post back to the previous
+revision's text and publishing again, which writes a new revision rather
+than erasing the old one.

+---

+
+# Revisions
+
+The Revisions screen lists every revision for a site, grouped by the post
+each one belongs to. Each group's heading uses the post's current title;
+each row uses the title that was saved at the moment of that publish, so
+renaming a post afterward doesn't rewrite what an older row says it
+published.
+
+A draft save updates the post without writing a revision. Only a publish
+adds one.
+
+## Ordering
+
+Revisions are listed newest first within a post. Two publishes in the same
+second are ordinary — the API breaks the tie by revision id, descending, so
+the more recently written revision still sorts first even when its
+timestamp exactly matches an earlier one.
+
+## Publishing and a failed hook
+
+A post becomes `published` together with the revision that snapshots it, in
+one transaction. A failed deploy hook doesn't touch either: the post stays
+published and its revision stays in place even when the site itself didn't
+rebuild. See [the publish contract and what a failed hook means](./publishing.md#what-a-failed-hook-does-and-doesnt-do)
+and [recovering a missed build](./guides/desk.md).
